name: Didjits
label: Touch and Go
lede: Rick Sims fronted the Didjits in sunglasses and a feather boa, with his brother Brad on drums, and made Touch and Go records that mostly ran under 30 minutes. One song, Killboy Powerhead, then rode the Offspring's Smash into more than 11 million homes.

eras.title: A railroad town and a Little Richard plan
eras.text: Mattoon is a railroad town in central Illinois. The first Didjits, a teenage band, didn't last; the second got good once Rick Sims stopped trying to please anyone. His plan, as he tells it: a modern Little Richard and Jerry Lee Lewis, played at punk speed.

years.big: "I had no idea what I was doing. I wasn't making music that I liked, music for myself."
years.h: Rick Sims and his brother Brad start a band in Mattoon, Illinois
years.p: Rick Sims on guitar and vocals, Brad Sims on drums, in a railroad town in central Illinois. That first line-up broke up, and Rick went on to UXB.
years.xp:
Between Didjits line-ups, Sims sang and played drums in UXB, with [[Doug Evans|17c6a990-b88b-4ed1-a11e-5d880c0a8c4b]] on guitar and Mike Rankin on bass. When the Didjits came back, Sims returned to guitar and Evans moved to bass.

UXB's tapes finally came out in 2024, on the bonus LP Bring Me the Head of Jaco Pastorius.

years.h: Fizzjob goes from first note to finished mix in 12 hours
years.p: Producer [[Iain Burgess|1572ff4f-9714-4d7e-804a-49b86a74a855]] cut the Didjits' debut at Chicago Recording Company, and the band put it out themselves on Bam Bam.
years.xp:
Rick Sims on the session: "in a 12-hour session from start to finish, the whole fucking record, from playing the first note to mixed and out the door."

Wikipedia and the AV Club date the record to 1986; Bandcamp Daily says 1987.

eras.title: Thanksgiving at Corey Rusk's
eras.text: A tape handed over at a holiday dinner got the Didjits onto Touch and Go, where they made their best-known records with Iain Burgess and a pseudonymous Steve Albini. One of those songs would travel much farther than the band did.

years.h: Over Thanksgiving turkey, Corey Rusk asks: "What the fuck is that?"
years.p: Steve Albini brought a tape of Hey Judester to Rusk's holiday dinner. Rusk and his wife Lisa, who had written the Didjits off as a novelty act, decided to release it.
years.xp:
Rick Sims remembers the double take: Rusk, and then his wife Lisa, both asking the same question. Albini went on to engineer several Didjits records under the pseudonym Reggie Stiggs. Hey Judester itself was produced by [[Iain Burgess|1572ff4f-9714-4d7e-804a-49b86a74a855]] and the band, and runs 26 minutes, with a cover of Little Richard's Lucille.

The press split. The Chicago Sun-Times called it the band's high point. The Toronto Star heard a pile of racial and sexist slurs, while granting the songs were meant as parody. On one Bay Area stop, Sims says, [[Jello Biafra|2280ca0e-6968-4349-8c36-cb0cbd6ee95f]] asked to record the set and the band's own sound man wouldn't allow it.

years.h: Killboy Powerhead debuts on Hornet Piñata, four years before Smash
years.p: The Didjits' second Touch and Go album carries the song that later lands on an album selling in the millions.

years.h: The three originals make Full Nelson Reilly, their last album together
years.p: Rick Sims, Doug Evans and Brad Sims record their third Touch and Go album.

years.h: Brad Sims leaves to raise a family
years.p: After Full Nelson Reilly, Brad Sims steps away from his brother's band. The Didjits carry on with borrowed drummers.

eras.title: Two drummers, a missing bassist and a breakaway bottle
eras.text: With Brad Sims gone the band drafted Rey Washam of Scratch Acid and Rapeman, then Todd Cole. The end came in Chicago: a night the bassist didn't show, and a stage skit the crowd hated.

yt: Full set at the Trocadero, Philadelphia, April 11, 1992
years.h: Rey Washam takes the drum stool for Little Miss Carriage!
years.p: Washam had drummed for [[Big Boys|fde1cff2-5a7b-4e8c-9666-110fa90500fb]], [[Scratch Acid|75687111-1585-4df2-83e6-ce52e7fa2bb0]] and [[Steve Albini|a4d486bd-6020-4a36-9c7d-bf5ce174bcd1]]'s [[Rapeman|899dea17-b403-42e0-9673-2623c40081af]] before he sat in on the Didjits' 1992 EP.
years.xp: Rick Sims says he got to know Washam at Touch and Go social gatherings. The stay was short: Todd Cole was on the next album.

years.p: The video airs on the MTV cartoon, and the band turns up on 120 Minutes. The album, the Didjits' last, has Todd Cole on drums, Steve Albini engineering and a [[Plasmatics|3fec8b00-4142-4129-96f5-1c9bf65e8e8f]] cover, Monkey Suit.

years.h: A breakaway bottle ends the Didjits in Chicago
years.p: At the final show, Rick Sims hit actor Joey Slotnick over the head with a bottle in a skit, and the crowd turned on them. A gig earlier, Doug Evans hadn't shown and [[Pierre Kezdy|061ef98c-497e-4a61-9464-10bf622c3c24]] of [[Pegboy|13e78eec-9ee4-47f2-a50e-2a9f519cb6e2]] had filled in on bass.
years.xp:
Sims on the skit: "It was a breakaway bottle and had fake blood in it." The audience didn't like it. His verdict: "That was the last show." The Didjits stayed quiet for twelve years.

The following year Sims joined the [[Supersuckers|6fa09822-bbe4-4ff8-901d-4a39a4dd82e9]], replacing guitarist Ron Heathman, and played on The Sacrilicious Sounds of the Supersuckers, produced by [[Paul Leary|976549ea-72bb-45ea-9431-3f07b4ed7dc8]] of the [[Butthole Surfers|2339bc21-aa92-4850-86f0-4bb9433910c8]].

years.h: A tape in a car puts Killboy Powerhead on Smash
years.p: While the Offspring recorded Smash, Chris Bagarozzi of Claw Hammer played them a Hornet Piñata tape in a car. Bandcamp Daily puts the album at 11 million-plus sold; Rick Sims says 14 million.
years.xp: Bandcamp Daily says Dexter Holland picked Killboy Powerhead off the tape for the album.

eras.title: Other bands, one reunion, one loss
eras.text: Rick Sims kept playing loud, in other people's bands and his own, from the Supersuckers to Gaza Strippers. The original three got back together once, for Touch and Go's birthday. Doug Evans moved to California and never stopped playing.

years.h: Rick Sims starts Gaza Strippers, then backs Fred Schneider
years.p: Gaza Strippers, with Darren Hooper and Todd Marino, make three albums through 2002 on Lookout! and Man's Ruin. Sims also plays behind [[Fred Schneider|43bcca8b-9edc-4997-8343-122350e790bf]] of the B-52's in Deadly Cupcake, on the Albini-produced Just... Fred.

years.cap: Drums at the Touch and Go 25th anniversary block party, Chicago, Sept 9, 2006
years.h: The original three play Touch and Go's 25th block party
years.p: Rick Sims, Doug Evans and Brad Sims play the Chicago block party, then a Champaign show the following weekend.

years.h: Doug Evans, the Didjits' bassist, dies in California at 53
years.p: Evans had been playing in Blöwer with his partner Merilee Kuchon. Rick Sims called him one of the most generous people he knew; plans for another reunion were shelved.
years.xp: The AV Club's obituary did not give a cause of death. Friends said he was happiest on his motorcycle, still playing music, and Corey Rusk remembered his skill and patience.

eras.title: Strictly dynamite
eras.text: Touch and Go boxed up the Didjits' best, UXB tapes and all, and Rick Sims put a new rhythm section together for the band's first shows in almost two decades.

years.h: Strictly Dynamite boxes the best of the Didjits, with a UXB bonus LP
years.p: Touch and Go's best-of comes with Bring Me the Head of Jaco Pastorius, which collects Rick Sims's earlier band UXB.
years.xp: UXB's tapes had sat unreleased since Sims, Doug Evans and Mike Rankin made them between Didjits line-ups.

yt: Didjits live at Riot Fest, Sept 19, 2025
years.h: Riot Fest brings the Didjits back with a new rhythm section
years.p: Rick Sims returns with Billy Fury, singer of Soy City Stranglers, on bass and Beanz, his cousin's son, on drums. They also play Chicago's Empty Bottle.
years.xp: Bandcamp Daily's interview has Riot Fest asking for the Didjits and Sims saying yes.

sources.title: Bandcamp Daily: Gassing Up the Didjits with Rick Sims (2025)
